originalRequest: Author a complete English course for the open Agent-courses site on orchestrating agents, slug learn-orchestrating-agents, closing a seven-course ladder. Target reader: fluent with a single agent, with tasks that have started outgrowing what one session can carry. Terminal task: decompose one real large task into parallelisable subtasks, run them, and produce a synthesis someone else can check. Six lessons: when NOT to use multiple agents; lead/worker with isolated contexts; why a subagent returns a summary rather than its whole transcript; serial versus parallel trade-offs and their failure modes; how a synthesiser avoids inventing a second layer of hallucination; running one real decomposition end to end. Lesson 1 must be genuinely willing to talk the reader out of multi-agent setups, carrying both Anthropic's simplest-solution-first position and Cognition's published argument against multi-agent architectures. Do not teach a specific orchestration framework's API. Pick up exactly where the context-engineering course's subagent lesson stops. Recency is a hard rule: every factual claim must come from a source fetched during the session.
learnerBrief: Someone who already runs an agent on real multi-step work and has hit the wall where a single session cannot carry a task: a migration across dozens of files, an audit of unfamiliar code, a research question with several independent threads. They can create files, run commands, and read agent output critically. They have most likely already tried spawning a second agent and found the results hard to trust or hard to assemble. What they need is not enthusiasm for multi-agent architectures but a decision procedure — when the split pays, what a worker actually needs, what comes back, what bounds concurrency, and how to write a result that survives someone else checking it. They should be able to finish the course having decided, on evidence from their own work, that some of their tasks do not warrant this apparatus at all.

briefCompleteness.evidence: The request supplied the audience ('fluent with a single agent; tasks have started outgrowing what one session can carry'), the terminal task ('decompose one real large task into parallelisable subtasks, run them, and produce a synthesis someone else can check'), the lesson count and all six themes, and three explicit scope boundaries: pick up exactly where agent-context-engineering lesson 5 stops without re-teaching context rot or the four levers, teach no orchestration framework's API, and cross-reference verify-agent-output rather than re-teaching verification. It further specified that Lesson 1 must be willing to argue against multi-agent setups and named the two positions that belong there. That is a starting point, an objective, and constraints — not a bare topic name.
briefCompleteness.assumptionsMade: Four judgment calls were made from evidence rather than asked, since the run was unattended. First, the ordering of the two first-hand incidents: concurrency collapse was placed in Lesson 4 where dispatch shape is decided, and the unverifiable completion reports in Lesson 5 where synthesis is written, because each incident is the strongest available illustration of that lesson's central claim. Second, the decision to present the four-question test, the three drop classes, and the four claim kinds as declared syntheses rather than dropping them: each component is separately sourced, and the lesson prose says in the body that the arrangement is the course's own. Third, British spelling throughout, matching the existing agent-readable-repo and verify-agent-output courses in this library. Fourth, the choice to cite MAST's per-mode prevalence figures despite their population being research frameworks on older models: the figures are used only to establish that coordination failures dominate, and every citation carries the population and model generation in the surrounding sentence.

learnerModel.targetReader: A developer or technical practitioner who runs a coding or research agent on real multi-step work daily, and has recently had a task fail because it did not fit in one session.
knownConcepts: Running an agent on a multi-step task and reading its output critically
Writing a task brief with a stated objective and acceptance criteria
That an agent's context window is finite and that a fuller window degrades performance
That a subagent runs in an isolated context and returns a summary — taught as a context-isolation device in the context-engineering course
Creating files, running commands, and reading a git diff
That an agent's completion claim is not evidence of completion — the premise of the verify-agent-output course
unknownConcepts: The orchestrator-worker pattern as an architecture, and where the plan, the results, and the stopping decision live in it
What a delegation brief must contain, and which failure each missing part produces
How to derive a dispatch shape from dependency structure rather than from piece count
That rate limits are organisation-wide and burst-sensitive, and that concurrency itself is a trigger
That a synthesis pass is a second, measured site of fabrication rather than an assembly step
Any specific orchestration framework's API, which the course deliberately never teaches
learnerModel.assumedEnvironment: The reader's own agent tool — any of them — their own repository or working directory, and a text file for briefs and notes. The course assumes no particular tool, no orchestration framework, no cloud account, no ability to install anything, and no team. Every exercise runs against work the reader already has. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.
learnerModel.firstIndependentAction: After Lesson 1, run the four-question test on three real tasks from their own list and reach a defended verdict on each — using only the test taught in that lesson, with no agent dispatched and nothing configured.
noviceRamp: The bridge from known to unknown starts at the reader's own stuck task and the move they were about to make, then spends the entire first lesson on the case against making it. No orchestration vocabulary appears until the reader has decided, on their own tasks, whether the apparatus applies.

The course picks up precisely where agent-context-engineering lesson 5 stops. That lesson taught a subagent as a context boundary and explicitly deferred orchestration; this course never re-derives context rot, the write/select/compress/isolate levers, or the coupling test, and instead starts from the fact that a worker's inheritance is a delegation message.

Every term follows the everyday-handle-then-formal-name order: 'the message the lead composes' before 'delegation brief', 'what comes back' before 'return channel', 'the report in the middle of the pile' before 'positional bias'.

The two first-hand incidents are introduced as bounded narratives with an explicit statement of what they do and do not show, so a reader learns the failure shape without generalising a single occurrence into a law.

Each lesson's exercises raise the environment requirement by exactly one step: Lesson 1 needs nothing but the reader's task list, Lesson 2 needs one worker, Lesson 3 needs a report they already have, Lesson 4 needs a small comparison run, Lesson 5 needs a synthesis to mark up, and Lesson 6 needs the full sequence. A reader with no delegation tooling at all can complete Lessons 1 and 3 from documents alone.
The terminal task is scoped to a read-only fan-out of three or four pieces, and Lesson 6 says explicitly why a first run should not also be a first experiment in parallel writes.

scope: Covers the decision of whether to split a task at all, including the published case against; the orchestrator-worker shape and where the plan, results and stopping decision live; the four documented parts of a delegation brief and the failure each absence produces; why the return channel is a condensed summary, the three classes of information that compression systematically drops, and when a result should be routed to a file instead; dependency structure as the input to dispatch shape, the illusion of divisibility, shared resources as the real bound on concurrency, blocking waves and wave sizing; and synthesis as a second measured site of fabrication, with the four-way claim marking, the case against extra merging layers, and verification against artifacts rather than reports. Deliberately excludes: any orchestration framework's API, SDK, or configuration syntax; context rot, the four context levers, and the coupling test, all of which belong to the agent-context-engineering course; how to build a verification gate, which belongs to verify-agent-output and is cross-referenced rather than repeated; agent-to-agent protocols; cost accounting beyond published order-of-magnitude figures; and running agents in production infrastructure.

evidence: Anthropic's engineering index was read in full on 2026-08-23 to establish what first-party material on this topic exists now; it surfaced two 2026 posts that no prior knowledge would have supplied — 'Building a C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes' (2026-02-05) and 'Harness design for long-running application development' (2026-03-24), both of which report measured multi-agent results and both of which are load-bearing for Lessons 4, 5 and 6.

The Cognition post was fetched at its current canonical host after the cognition.ai URL was found to 301-redirect to cognition.com; the redirect was confirmed during the session and sources.md records the final address, which returns 200 without redirect.

The MAST paper's arXiv record was read on 2026-08-23 and shows v3, last revised 2025-10-26, published in the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks track — a later and larger version (1600+ traces) than the v1 abstract that circulates in secondary write-ups, and the per-mode prevalence figures were taken from the current full text rather than from any summary.

The Claude Code subagents and agent-teams documentation pages were fetched as raw markdown on 2026-08-23; the agent-teams page self-describes as covering v2.1.178 and states that the feature is experimental and disabled by default, which is why the course teaches the lead/worker shape and mentions peer teams only as a contrast.

The OpenAI Codex subagents documentation was fetched on 2026-08-23 and provides the cross-vendor confirmation used in Lesson 1 and the read-heavy-first rule used in Lesson 4; the canonical developers.openai.com path currently serves the learn.chatgpt.com URL recorded in sources.md.
All fifteen source URLs were checked programmatically on 2026-08-23 under the same fetch semantics the guard uses, and all returned 200 with no redirect.
topicCurrency.staleRisk: This course was written to age slowly and parts of it will still age. Ages first: the two vendor documentation sources. The agent-teams page is explicitly experimental and version-stamped at v2.1.178, and its limitations list is the most perishable material cited anywhere in the course; the Codex subagents page is versioned rather than dated. Both are cited for mechanism rather than for click-paths, so a change in either is likely to invalidate a detail rather than a lesson. Ages second: the token and cost figures. The 15x multiple, the 4x chat multiple, and the 9-dollars-versus-200-dollars comparison are all measurements of specific 2025 and 2026 workloads on specific model generations, and every one carries its setting in the prose — but a reader in a year should expect the ratios to have moved. Ages third: the 90.2% internal-eval figure, which is bound to Claude Opus 4 as lead and Sonnet 4 as subagents and is already a historical measurement. Ages fourth: the MAST prevalence percentages, whose population is GPT-4-era and Claude-3-era research frameworks; the taxonomy will outlast the numbers. Ages fifth: the summarisation-hallucination and positional-bias findings, both measured on GPT-4o-era models — the U-shape and the merging result are mechanism-level and should survive, the rates should not be carried forward. Ages slowest, and deliberately so: the decomposition reasoning, the four-part brief, the dependency-structure-before-concurrency ordering, the shared-resource argument, and the claim-marking discipline in Lesson 5, none of which depend on any product's behaviour. The two first-hand incidents do not age at all in the sense that matters, because they are dated observations from one build and are presented as such rather than as claims about how systems behave in general.
topicCurrency.recheckProcedure: Open Anthropic's engineering index and check for posts newer than 2026-03-24 on orchestration, harness design, or parallel agents; that index is where the two most valuable 2026 sources for this course were found. Then re-fetch the two vendor documentation pages and diff their guidance on parallel dispatch and token cost against Lessons 3, 4 and 6 — the agent-teams limitations list first, since it is experimental. Then check whether MAST has a newer revision with a changed trace population. The lesson content that would need rewriting if any of these moved is named in staleRisk in priority order.

qualitySelfReview.diagramUse: One mermaid diagram, in Lesson 2: a lead fanning out to three workers and their summaries converging on a synthesis. It earns its place because the lesson's central structural claim — that every arrow passes through the lead and the workers never touch each other — is the thing that makes two workers' incompatible assumptions invisible until synthesis, and that is a statement about topology that costs a paragraph in prose and one glance as a diagram. It carries a sentence after it naming exactly what to look for. No diagram was used elsewhere and each omission was deliberate: Lesson 1's material is a decision test, better served by the four-row table that is already there; Lesson 3's asymmetry is a ratio, carried by the numbers themselves; Lesson 4's content is three dependency relationships and a list of shared resources, both of which are handled by short labelled text blocks that also show the reasoning, which a diagram would hide; Lesson 5's four claim kinds are a table because they are a classification rather than a structure; and Lesson 6's sequence is a numbered list where each step carries the failure it prevents, which a flowchart would strip out. A second diagram in Lesson 4 was drafted and cut — it showed three dispatch shapes side by side and duplicated the worked example without adding a relationship the text does not state.
weakestPoints: The outline came pre-set from the design brief — six lessons against six named themes, in a fixed order — and was auto-confirmed in a non-interactive run. No human reviewed the lesson order, the coverage, or the depth before any prose was written. The prerequisite DAG was checked mechanically and the load balanced (roughly 195 to 240 non-code lines per lesson, six to seven new concepts each), but if the intended reader wanted, say, more on peer-to-peer coordination and less on synthesis, nothing in this run would have surfaced that.

Three of the course's organising structures are the author's own syntheses rather than findings from any source: the four-question test in Lesson 1, the three drop classes in Lesson 3, and the four claim kinds in Lesson 5. Each is assembled from separately cited findings and each is declared as a synthesis in the lesson body. But none has been validated against anyone's real practice, and a reader whose task does not decompose along those axes could follow all three precisely and still make a bad call. The four-question test is the most exposed, because it is the first thing the course asks anyone to do and it presents a genuinely fuzzy judgment as four binary answers.

The terminal task cannot be verified by the author, and its success criterion is unusually soft. Lesson 6 asks the reader to produce a synthesis another person can audit, and the check is that a reader names a claim and says how they would check it. That is self-reported, and a reader who does the reader test with a friendly colleague will pass it whatever they wrote. The instruction to use a fresh agent session with no context is the strongest available substitute and is still not a real audit.

The two first-hand incidents are single observations from one build with no root cause established for either. The concurrency collapse is especially thin as evidence: five workers hit 500s and re-running serially worked, which is consistent with a rate limit, an acceleration limit, a transient gateway fault, or coincidence. The lesson says explicitly that the cause was never established and draws only the structural conclusion about blast radius — but a reader could still come away believing parallel dispatch caused those specific failures, which the evidence does not support.

The course teaches decomposition without teaching any tooling, by design, and this leaves a real gap at exactly one point. A reader whose agent tool has no delegation mechanism at all can do the reasoning in every lesson and cannot run the fan-out in Lessons 4 and 6. The exercises are written so Lessons 1, 2, 3 and 5 work with manual parallel sessions, but Lesson 4's serial-versus-parallel comparison assumes the reader can dispatch several workers somehow, and the course never says what to do if they cannot.

The published evidence for the central positive claim is thinner than its prominence suggests, and the course leans on one organisation for much of it. Six of the fifteen sources are Anthropic engineering posts. The 90.2% figure, the 15x multiple, the sizing tiers, the blocking bottleneck and the filesystem pattern all come from a single post about a single product. The independent evidence — MAST, the two summarisation papers — is largely about failure rather than about what works, so the course's account of successful orchestration rests more heavily on first-party vendor reporting than its account of failure does. This is stated where it matters in the prose, but it is a real asymmetry in the evidence base.

Lesson 5's cross-reference to the verify-agent-output course assumes the reader has done it or will. The lesson names the prerequisite habit and moves on, which is correct for a ladder but leaves a reader arriving at this course cold with a two-sentence version of a six-lesson subject at exactly the point where the course's most consequential advice sits.
followUpChecks: Have the user review the outline — lesson order, coverage, depth — since it was auto-confirmed in a non-interactive run, and revise if the emphasis is wrong.

Watch what happens when a reader applies the four-question test to a task where the honest answer to Q1 is 'partly'. The test forces a binary answer and real tasks are often mixed; if readers routinely round, the test needs a third verdict rather than a sharper Q1.
Re-open Anthropic's engineering index for material published after 2026-03-24. That index was where the two most valuable 2026 sources for this course were found, and the topic is moving.

Re-fetch the agent-teams documentation and diff its limitations list against Lesson 2's contrast between lead/worker and peer coordination. It is experimental, version-stamped, and the most perishable thing cited in the course.

Find an independent, non-vendor measurement of when multi-agent decomposition actually outperforms a single session on coding tasks specifically. The course currently has to say that most coding tasks are not the shape the published gains came from, citing the vendor whose gain it is, and better evidence either way would strengthen Lesson 1 considerably.

Have a reader attempt Lesson 6's terminal task and hand the synthesis to a genuinely uninvolved person. Find out whether the four claim marks survive contact with someone who did not write them, or whether 'verified' quietly absorbs 'I was confident'.

acceptanceReview.scoreNotes: structure 5: all six lessons carry objectives, a lesson-specific hook heading, an explanation section, a worked example, a faded example with answers, exercises, and a closing heading that differs from every other lesson's; the README table and the Prev/Next chain are complete and the prerequisite DAG is clean, with each lesson using only what earlier lessons established. grounded 5: fifteen sources, every one fetched and read in full during this session, all fifteen returning 200 without redirect under the guard's own fetch semantics; every volatile figure carries its workload, model generation, or publication date in the sentence that uses it, and the two first-hand incidents are labelled as single observations with an explicit statement of what they do not show. pedagogy 4 rather than 5: the worked-to-faded-to-independent ladder holds in all six lessons and the concrete-to-abstract ordering is genuine, but Lesson 1 asks for a judgment the reader has no experience to ground yet — the four-question test is applied before they have seen a fan-out succeed or fail — and Lesson 6's success criterion depends on a reader they must find themselves. exercises 4: every exercise has approach guidance, measurable completion criteria, a reference answer, and progressive hints, and four of the twelve carry explicit common-mistake breakdowns; held at 4 because every verification is self-report in the reader's own environment and the Level 2 exercises in Lessons 4 and 6 require running the same work twice, which some readers will not do. load 4: six to seven new concepts per lesson against a cap of about seven, so the course sits at the top of its band rather than comfortably inside it; lesson lengths are balanced at roughly 195 to 240 non-code lines with no outlier, and the glossary's 83 entries across six lessons (13.8 per lesson) sits inside the target band with every term appearing verbatim in the prose. readable 4: prose is chunked into short self-contained blocks and every citation sits under the sentence it supports, but Lesson 4 carries an unavoidable density of mechanism — dependency structure, divisibility, shared resources, blocking, and wave sizing in one lesson — and is the hardest reading in the course.
acceptanceReview.terminalTask: The reader takes one real task from their own work, runs the four-question test on it, draws its dependency structure and creates any missing shared artifact, writes a four-part brief with a return format containing locators and an uncertainty slot, dispatches a small first wave chosen against blast radius rather than speed, verifies every completion claim against the artifacts before writing anything, and produces a synthesis in which every claim is marked verified, reported, contested, or inferred, with a method-notes section recording what went wrong and what was spot-checked. The deliverable is then handed to another person — or a fresh agent session with no context — who must be able to name a claim they would check and say how, without asking the reader anything.
acceptanceReview.interactionCheck: Three body interaction blocks across six lessons, plus three agentmentor-action cards, which is deliberately sparse for a course whose subject is judgment rather than syntax. Lesson 1, agentmentor-check 'Judge which task earns a second agent': serves the specific misconception the whole course exists to correct — that task size is the criterion for splitting. All four options are tasks a reader would plausibly split, and the three wrong ones fail on different axes (invisible shared convention, sequential dependence, coupling to session context), so the block tests the dependency reasoning rather than recall of a rule. Lesson 3, agentmentor-check 'Read what a clean report leaves out': serves the not-found class, which is the one drop class that is undetectable from the report itself; the distractor most readers pick is the missing locator, which is real but recoverable, whereas the correct answer names the absence that cannot be recovered after the worker's context is gone. Lesson 5 carries no body interaction block, which is a deliberate choice: its central skill is marking a real document, and the faded example already has the reader classify five claims against three reports with reference answers — a check block there would have been a weaker version of the exercise sitting immediately below it. Lessons 2, 4 and 6 also carry no check block; in each case the judgment being taught is too situated to reduce to a multiple choice without becoming a giveaway, and each has a faded example that does the same work with the reader's own reasoning. The three action cards are lesson-specific training moves rather than generic buttons: Lesson 1's is a reasoning audit that attacks the reader's own split decision and is explicitly forbidden from helping them plan the decomposition; Lesson 4's is a pressure scenario that kills the reader's planned fan-out partway through and makes them describe the wreckage before offering anything; Lesson 6's is a teach-back that walks the reader's own finished synthesis claim by claim and demands the command behind every 'verified' mark. Lessons 2, 3 and 5 carry no action card, keeping overall density at roughly one interaction per lesson.
acceptanceReview.learnerFitCheck: Targets a practitioner who is fluent with one agent and has just hit the wall where a task does not fit in one session — someone who has probably already tried a second agent and found the result hard to trust. Four hidden prerequisites were removed. First, no orchestration framework: the course teaches decomposition, delegation and failure modes and never names an API, so a reader on any tool can do all the reasoning. Second, no re-derivation of context engineering: the course picks up exactly where agent-context-engineering lesson 5 stopped, taking the isolated context window and the summary return as given rather than re-teaching context rot or the four levers. Third, no verification apparatus: Lesson 5 needs the reader to distrust a completion claim, and rather than building that from scratch it names the habit, gives the two first-hand incidents as concrete evidence, and points at the verify-agent-output course for the full treatment. Fourth, no team: every exercise runs against work the reader already has, alone, and the one place a second person is genuinely needed — Lesson 6's reader test — offers a fresh agent session as an equivalent. The first independent action is running the four-question test on three real tasks, which needs nothing installed, nothing dispatched, and no vocabulary beyond what Lesson 1 teaches; the reader's own task list is the entire input. Each subsequent lesson raises the environment requirement by exactly one step, and a reader whose tool cannot dispatch workers at all can still complete Lessons 1, 2, 3 and 5 against documents and manual sessions.
promotionNotes: Before promotion to examples/, re-fetch the two vendor documentation sources. The agent-teams page is experimental and version-stamped at v2.1.178, and its limitations list is the most perishable material cited in the course; the Codex subagents page is versioned rather than dated.

The four-question test, the three drop classes, and the four claim kinds are the course's own syntheses and are labelled as such in the prose. If they survive contact with several readers' real tasks, they are worth keeping as they stand; if readers routinely find their tasks do not decompose along those axes, that is a signal to rework them rather than to defend them.

The evidence base leans on one organisation for the positive case — six of fifteen sources are Anthropic engineering posts, and the central figures in Lesson 1 all come from one of them. An independent measurement of when decomposition beats a single session, particularly on coding tasks, would materially strengthen Lesson 1 and should be sought before this course is held up as an example of grounding.

The two first-hand incidents are the course's most distinctive material and also its least corroborated. They are presented as single observations from one build with no established cause, which is honest. If a similar failure is observed again in this project, the record should be updated with the second occurrence rather than the original claim being strengthened.

No temporary slug, no placeholder text, no TODOs. All fifteen source URLs returned 200 without redirect when checked on 2026-08-23 under the guard's own fetch semantics, and every glossary term was verified to appear verbatim in the numbered lesson files.
